It is from the Padinska Skela correction facility in Belgrade, where it says that on the 13th of January, 2000, you escaped from serving your prison sentence. You were allowed to go home to visit your family, but you failed to return. Do you remember that escape from prison? Now, escaping from prison isn't a crime where we come from; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-033
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Well, they could have just put you in a solitary confinement cell.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-033
utterances.text: Well, that's what they did. They did put me in a solitary confinement cell.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Let's move on to number 20 because I don't have much time.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreters kindly request that the speaker be asked to slow down.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Both of you, the interpreters are having great difficulties in following the speed of your speech, and it goes for both you, Mr. Seselj, and for the witness. Thanks.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could you tell me how much time I have left, because I'd like to go through all the documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ms. Registrar, how much time do we have left, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You have 19 minutes left.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: So this is an indictment that was issued against you by the District Public Prosecutor's Office in Belgrade on the 3rd of June, 1996. Your name is mentioned here, and there is another co-accused. And everything that was noted in the criminal report is repeated here, all the crimes; the mosque, the bombs that were planted under the cars and under the windows of the apartment owned by this Albanian person, then all the stuff that was found at your place. So this is the indictment that was issued against you. Do you remember this indictment?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-033
utterances.text: Well, I assume that that is it. I'm not sure. I never signed anything of the sort, but I assume that it is, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: You should know that you do not sign the indictment. You are served with the indictment, and you just signed the accompanying paper.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-033
utterances.text: Well, we don't have faxes in prison. The police comes in, gives it to you, and you put it in the pocket. That's how it's done in Serbia so that I probably had this in my possession, but -- well, I don't know exactly what it is, but I probably should have received an indictment if I ended up in prison.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Please, please, sir, Witness VS-033, I did time in Serbian jails, not for terrorism, not for crime, but for political crimes. Every time the prison guards bring you a document from the court, from the Prosecutor's Office, you receive a blue sheet of paper where you sign confirming that you received it. So you don't sign the document itself, you sign a blue piece of paper. It's as if every time you receive the summons, you do the same thing. Please, don't go on attacking the Serbian judicial system. If anyone has the right to do that, because of everything they did to me over the past decades, it's me. So now we have document number 21. It's the beginning of the trial. Could we please have it all on the ELMO, just to have a chance to look at it. So this is the record of the trial. We see, on the next page, the basic formalities are observed, and then the first accused was questioned, and at page 4 of this document, that's page 23 of this set of documents, we can see what you, yourself, stated in court, as the accused was examined. In our legal system, once the trial begins, the accused are the first to give statements, and then witnesses are called and evidence is adduced. Here, in this record, it is indicated that you received the indictment that you now don't remember, that you were able to understand the contents, and that you were presenting your defence in the presence of your defence counsel. I will not be giving his name, but I know him personally. It is stated for the record that the accused presented his defence as he did in the record of the interview with the Investigative Judge on the 22nd of April, 1996; is that right? So it is stated for the record, and let us now see what statement we're talking about, what interview we're talking about, the date is the 22nd of April. That would be the one where you confess to everything. So first you confess to everything before an Investigating Judge, then you avail yourself of the right to remain silent, then in May you denied some elements. But faced with everything that the Prosecution had against you, you now confirm the first statement that you gave to the Investigating Judge, and you go on to say that the crime listed under -- in count 1, and that is the bomb at the mosque, that you did it in order to fulfill the wishes of your comrade, Vlada -- well, I'm not going to mention his last name. But, at any rate, somebody made this last wish, the dying wish to you. And then you go on to say who was your accomplice or co-perpetrator, and then you confirm that the quantity of weapons listed in the certificate was indeed found at your place. And then you say: "I explain all that by the fact that at that time I believed that it was much better for me to cause sound effects by my acts than to have a massacre in Belgrade." So your justification for your act is that it was better for you to cause controlled explosions at the mosque and at Catholic churches than for somebody else, who didn't know how to do it, to do it in such a way that it resulted in such a massacre. So this was your justification, the way you justified your acts before the Court; is that so, Mr. VS-033?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-033
utterances.text: Yes, that's what I say -- said, probably.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: And then the next sentence: "I believe that all kinds of things would have happened had it not been for me causing those sound effects, because the wounded people were coming in from the frontline and they were visited by a number of volunteers and they talked about all kinds of things." So you are saying that your bomb attacks, your terrorist acts, resulted in saving the mosque, the Catholic Church, and the cars and this apartment owned by this Albanian man, because had somebody else had done it, it would have been much worse. So you did it, and those others who may have wanted to do that no longer wanted to do that because this had already been done. Is this the gist of what you said?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-033
utterances.text: Well, I was visited by my lawyer in jail, and I had to consult him about what I would say before the Court. It says here that I was represented by my Defence counsel.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Does it mean that you were influenced by your Defence counsel when you said that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-033
utterances.text: Well, I don't remember. I might say that I was under the influence of my Defence counsel, but we discussed the act. He came to visit me while I was in custody during the investigation.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Fair enough. But you now mention the blowing up of a bus in the last passage?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-033
utterances.text: Well, it says in the same passage that my lawyer silenced me and told me to sit down and to keep quiet.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Well, it's not mentioned here.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-033
utterances.text: Well, it is recorded here.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Well, it may have happened, but it is not reflected in the record. But at any rate, if your lawyer did tell you to keep quiet, in the last passage you talk about blowing up some bus, that some bus should be destroyed, saying it would be better for a bus to be destroyed than for it to fall in the enemy hands, so what are you talking about?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-033
utterances.text: Well, they might have recorded this in that manner. What I said was that we volunteers had had grenades when we went to the frontline. This was so that we could blow up the whole bus and ourselves if we fell into the enemy hands. The recording clerk probably noted this down in this manner to keep it shorter. And then my lawyer told me to keep quiet, and I never said anything else in front of the Judges.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: I have a feeling that your lawyer told you to keep quiet and then -- so lest you should incriminate yourself any further, and that's why it remained unclarified, what happened to this bus that was blown up.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: I'm not sure where Mr. Seselj is going with this line of questioning, but to the extent that this violates the attorney-client privilege ...

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, Judges, there is no confidentiality. I think everything is clear to you, and I'm not mentioning the name of this lawyer. I can bring you his statement here tomorrow, but because I respect the lawyer-client privilege, I will not be asking him to do that. I know this man, but I'm just trying to bring to your attention that there is this interesting incident in which the bus was blown up, but we don't know what that was all about. Could we move on to the next page.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What year are we talking about?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is the 1996 trial for the crimes committed in 1992, 1993 and 1994. So that's in continuity.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I didn't understand the question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We are talking about the fact that you allegedly took part in placing an explosive inside a bus, to destroy that bus. What I wanted to know: That particular event, the last one we spoke about, what year did that take place in?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I explained to the Court in Serbia how we went to the front lines and how we had those explosive devices or, rather, hand grenades that we were to use to blow up the bus if the bus were to fall into the enemy hands, because we volunteers, we were not armed as we travelled to the front line. We were supposed to blow up the bus in order to prevent ourselves falling into the enemy hands alive. Now, I'm not clear why this thing was reflected in the record in this way. This is what I explained to the Judges when they asked me how I knew to handle the explosives. And then I went on to explain to them that we had those hand grenades as we went to the front line on the bus. I don't know why this was reflected in this way.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All I wanted to know was what event you were talking about -- or, rather, the events you're talking about, what date? What is the timeline for those events, the battlefields, et cetera? Are we talking about the year when the war was on or not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As for the bus, that was in 1991. That's when we had those hand grenades, because the Judges were asking me questions when I was the accused in that case.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Madam Judge, it doesn't say here in the record "hand grenades," but it says "explosives," and the recording clerk cannot make such a mistake, he cannot write down "hand grenades" if he hears "explosives," and the other way around. I would just like to bring that to your attention. In the course of this trial, we don't need to read through the whole record --

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: -- you were sentenced to three years in prison, and the statement of reasons in the judgement explained why. You received that at a later stage. Could we now please have document number 23 up on the screen.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction: 22.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, let me take this advantage of this pause to ask you a question, Witness. What is the Serbian Volunteer Humanitarian Fund, exactly?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, at that time I was going to this fund, it was run by Dobrila and Milos Kustudic. They were also members of the -- or he was also of a member of the Radical Party. And on Saturdays and Sundays, we went there to help the wounded, to take fruit and cigarettes to them. They were hospitalised. There were many of them hospitalised all over Serbia, and nobody came to visit them, nobody took care of them, so that's what we did. We went to visit them, to visit the wounded volunteers and to help them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. So it was a humanitarian organisation rather than one involved in military operations?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Humanitarian organisation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, in that case, there's something I don't understand. You said that you left the Serbian Radical Party at a given date. Can you remind me what date that was, please?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes. That was in 1992.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And then you were part of this humanitarian organisation, so if I've understood you correctly, but I want you to confirm this, if that is the case, so simultaneously you organised these attacks, using explosives, so I would like to know on behalf of whom -- what type of organisation you belonged to, if at the same time if perhaps you were a member of a unit of volunteers under a different organisation, since you had left the Serbian Radical Party. There's something in the way you've told this that I don't understand.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This humanitarian organisation shares the premises with the Serbian Chetnik Movement at the Palilula Municipality on Preradoviceva Street. At that time, it shared premises, and both the humanitarian organisation, the Serbian Volunteers, and the Serbian Chetnik Movement were in the same office.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I continue?

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Do you know who gave those state-owned premise for the use of those various organisations? Who was it that allocated those premises?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-033
utterances.text: Probably the municipality.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: So an organisation gets registered, makes an application to the municipality. The municipality senses the public benefit and then allocates some offices for the use of that organisation?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-033
utterances.text: Probably.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: So now we've come to this judgement against you. That's document 22. This is a lengthy judgement. It contains a detailed description of everything that you did. There's no need, I hope -- do you recognise this judgement? There is no need for us to quote from it, because that would be just repetitive. This is all those elements that were contained in the criminal report and in the trial record. It says here that you were sentenced to three years in prison. Could you confirm that and confirm that this judgement is authentic and your accomplice was sentenced to two years?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-033
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: So there's no need for us to dwell on this document. Your Defence counsel appealed against this judgement; is that so?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-033
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: And then a ruling on the appeal filed by your Defence counsel, the Supreme Court of Serbia. On the 25th of December, 1997. You were present there at the session of the Supreme Court?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-033
utterances.text: No, I was not present.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Well, it says here that you were. It says here that you and your co-accused and your defence counsel were present there on the 25th of December, 1997.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-033
utterances.text: Well, yes, that was at the end of the investigation so that's probably when it was held.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Well, fine. The Supreme Court did grant some points of appeal of your accomplice but your -- and his sentence was commuted, but your sentence remained as it was, your appeal was dismissed; is that so?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-033
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: So there's no need for us to dwell on this anymore. I have a document here that shows that the government of the Republic of Serbia, as early as 2006, at the request of the Ministry of Foreign Affairs of the Republic of Serbia, obtained this document, which was then sent to the Federal Council for Cooperation with The Hague Tribunal. I have no evidence of that, but it should have been submitted to the Prosecution at the Tribunal, because this only proves that the whole procedure was complied with in the disclosure of these documents. The OTP did submit three potentially incriminating documents against you, but I don't have any evidence of that. Let us move on to document number 25. This is a file from a visit to the scene. This was done by the forensic technicians section from the Secretariat of the Interior in Belgrade. This is not very clear, but I hope that you will, I hope, recognise this is a reconstruction. You're showing how you went to the church of St. Anthony in the Pop Stojan Street, number 13, how the bomb was planted, and then you indicate the entrance to the church where you actually activated the explosive device, and then the next page. Do you remember this reconstruction of the incident at the scene?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-033
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: So you do confirm this?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-033
utterances.text: Yes. Well, the police put me in the car and just took me there.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: On the next page, again you show the yard of the church where you planted the bomb, and then you show how you lobbed the device over the fence. You can see that your hand is up in the air. You demonstrated that to the police. The next page, you can see a photograph of a building in Vojvoda Milanka [phoen] Street, where you planted this explosive device underneath the window of this Albanian man? Do you remember that? You here at the scene, do remember that you were showing that to the police, that this was when this photograph was taken?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-033
utterances.text: It was a long time ago, but probably, yes, they took me there in order for me to show them. They handcuffed me, put me in a car. They took me there, and there on the spot they took my handcuffs off so they could take pictures of me showing all this.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: On the photograph at the bottom of the page, you are bending down and indicating where precisely you placed the explosive. Your accomplice is there with you, but as these photographs are not very clear, it won't reveal his identity. Will you please turn the page now. This is again the entrance to the house in Gospadare Jenema [phoen] Street, number 13, where you put together the explosive device. Do you remember this, showing them this?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-033
utterances.text: Yes, yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: And the photograph at the lower half of the page is -- shows you indicating where you placed an explosive in front of the only mosque in Belgrade, the mosque there, Bajrakli Mosque?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-033
utterances.text: Probably that's how it was. The photograph is not very clear, but, yes, that's how it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Well, these photographs were faxed to me, they come from the court records, so I was unable to get hold of the original photographs, because had your testimony been announced to me in time, I would have been able to obtain these original photographs. The next page, the first photograph, here you are showing the path between the houses along which you went to the house in Nova Street, number 33. The street was 118th Nova, and the house number was 33. Do you remember this, when you crossed the meadow?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-033
utterances.text: Well, the photograph is not clear, but I know I was taken -- I and Gajic were taken to show this.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: The photograph underneath, you're showing the place where you stood and where there was a car covered by a canvass tarpaulin, where you planted the explosive device. You thought the vehicle belonged to an Albanian. In fact, it belonged to a Serb, but terrorism is terrorism. Do you remember this? If you don't recall, we'll move on. The next page, please. Here you're showing the police from where you came to the parking lot in front of Sutjeska Company on 22nd of November Street; is that right? Is this the parking lot?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-033
utterances.text: It looks like it. It probably is.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: The photograph in the lower half of the page, you show where the Renault car was parked underneath which you planted an explosive device; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-033
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Next page, please. Here you're indicating the place and the manner in which you planted and activated explosive device under a Renault car on the 29th of November Street. You're bending down here, showing how you did it; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-033
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Please turn to the next page.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-033
utterances.text: But --

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Here you're showing the place where a device exploded which you threw into the yard of the Church of St. Anthony on Pop Stojan Street; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-033
utterances.text: Probably, but I can't see this image very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: And we saw in your third statement to the Investigating Judge, you attempted to deny that you had thrown a hand grenade into the yard of St. Anthony's Church, but here you're showing how you did all this. So you lied to the Investigating Judge on that occasion?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-033
utterances.text: Well, in Serbia, when the police take you somewhere, you can't say anything. If they had taken me somewhere else, where a crime had been committed, I would have had to show them that I did it.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Oh, Mr. VS-033, please don't interrupt me. I spent time in various Yugoslav prisons, eight times, and it wasn't as bad as you're trying to make out. You're trying to make out you were in a prison run by Idi Amin or Bokassa. You're here showing what you did. You confessed to your crime, you admitted it, you're admitting it now, so what is it that the police coerced from you? Nothing.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-033
utterances.text: Well, what I'm trying to say is that had they taken me to other places, I would have had to say I'd done it, because the police are the supreme authority in Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Are you denying that you committed any of these crimes?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-033
utterances.text: No, I'm not denying anything now. I'm just trying to explain what the system is like in Serbia. I didn't deny it. Yes, this is a picture showing me indicating what was done.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Well, let's not discuss the system in Serbia now. On these photographs, we see you showing how you committed crimes, and you actually did commit these crimes? There's not a single detail here showing that you were taken somewhere where you had not committed a crime, at least not in this file; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-033
utterances.text: Okay, yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, please be kind enough to tell me how much time I have left. I have two important matters to deal with, so I have to distribute my time properly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, time is almost up. You have 60 seconds left, so please come to your conclusion.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If I may put one more question.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Even after this crime you committed, for which you were convicted and sentenced, I received information from the Office of the National Council for Cooperation with the International Criminal Tribunal for the former Yugoslavia, and the number of the document is listed here. It was sent on the 12th of February, 2008, and ex officio I asked this National Council to inspect your criminal record, and they informed me, under item 8 of that decision, first, that you had been convicted for these crimes, and, secondly, that you then committed a number of crimes, including forging a document. You forged a personal identity card. The OTP has disclosed to me a document showing that you had forged a personal identity card. And then you committed another crime under -- various crimes, Article 166, Article 171, and all these crimes that you committed after 1996 were forgiven you [as interpreted]. I have a document here disclosed to me by the OTP, saying that the Statue of Limitations was applied to some of them, and all this was because you're testifying in these proceedings against me; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-033
utterances.text: No, it's not correct.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter notes she did not catch the crimes that the witness allegedly committed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, I have a question, a follow-up question. Unless we were wrong, because of course we could make mistakes, but we had understood that you left the Serbian Radical Party and its volunteers in 1992, and we're finding out a document coming from your country's judicial authority which states that for several years, 1992, 1993, 1994, you committed a number of attacks using explosives. The dates are in document 18, page 2; the summer of December 8th, 1992; April 27, 1993; September 10, 1993; February 1st, 1994. Any reasonable judge would wonder who you committed these very serious acts for, on behalf of whom you committed these serious acts. These were perpetrated against religious places, mosques or churches, against property, cars and so on. So did you act on your own behalf or were you acting on behalf of some kind of organisation?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-033
utterances.text: At that time, I continued socialising and associating with volunteers from the Serbian Chetnik Movement and the Radical Party, and anyone who comes back from the war theatre suffers from a syndrome, and this syndrome remains there for a long time. The state didn't want to integrate us into society and help us. In fact, it hindered us, and we had to struggle with the syndrome on our own. And some people never got cured of the syndrome.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is your explanation? Very well. But my question was more specific. Did you act within an organisation or on your own behalf, being motivated by a post-traumatic syndrome that was a consequence of which you lived through in the war?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-033
utterances.text: Throwing a hand grenade on a mosque was because a friend of mine had stated the day before that it was his last wish. I didn't even know there was a mosque in Belgrade until he told me that in hospital. And that evening, he died. Nurse Ruska informed us that Vlada had died and that had been his dying wish, so we fulfilled it. We threw the hand grenade, not into the mosque itself but into the yard of the mosque. We didn't throw it inside, but into the yard, in order to avoid injuring anyone.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It seemed that this syndrome had lingered for quite a while. The search that was carried out in your home some years later where an arsenal was found, because earlier we read about what was in that arsenal. So why did you keep all this in your own home, given the fact -- you see, given the fact that this was found out in 1996?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-033
utterances.text: Yes. Little by little, in time -- over time, I brought it back from the war front and it was in my flat. And when the police entered my flat to arrest me, they found all these things.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] When you contacted the OTP following the invitation made by Mr. Petkovic, did you tell the OTP about all this, i.e., that you had planted explosive devices for years and so forth and so on? Did you tell them everything, did you do a mia copa?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-033
utterances.text: Yes, I told them everything sincerely and honestly. I told them I had done all this. The first time an indictment was raised against me, I've lost it now, I don't have it anymore, but it listed everything I had done.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] One last question. Tell me where you work. Could you tell me whether today you have a job?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] At the moment, I am not doing anything, I'm not employed. Until recently, I was a tinsmith, and I worked as a private entrepreneur on construction sites.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Up until which year did you have a job?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Until the end of 1997. No, sorry, 2007. I do apologise, 2007, until December. It's seasonal work. In summer, there's work. In winter, there isn't so much work. There is some, but far less. This is work you have to do outdoors, on roofs. You have to do various kinds of pipes and ducts on the roof and on the facade. So when it's snowing or raining, you can't work.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So for three months, you've been without a job. Well, what do you live on?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I am under the protection of the protection team.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What is this protection team?

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Your Honour, perhaps it might be a good time to go into private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Let's move to a private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we are back in open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ms. Biersay, do you have any redirect?

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: I do, Your Honour. I am uncertain whether the Court would like me to do it now or after the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We'll have a break, and we'll resume at 1.00, and we'll have 45 minutes left.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. We'll wait for Mr. Seselj. It is now time for the redirect.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I intend to cover three brief topics. One, the issue of the grenade and the bus, the conviction for recent -- recent convictions of the witness, and then, thirdly, asking some questions related to threats. And for that third topic, I will request that we move into private session.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Mr. Witness, you received some questions about grenades related to a bus. Do you recall those questions? Yes or no, please.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-033
utterances.text: Yes, I remember.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Do you recall the occasion on which you had grenades on a bus?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-033
utterances.text: That was in 1991, when we were setting out to Western Slavonia. Radonoci [phoen] distributed hand grenades to us in case we were taken prisoner on the way, because he was the only one who had a pistol. The rest of us were unarmed. And it was our duty to blow up the bus, together with the volunteers, if we were captured so as to avoid falling into enemy hands alive.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: And, Mr. Witness, did you describe that occasion in paragraph 15 of your 2006 statement to the ICTY? And for your reference, you have the statements in front of you.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-033
utterances.text: In what paragraph?

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Paragraph 15 of the 2006.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-033
utterances.text: Yes, that's what I was referring to in paragraph 15.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Seselj asked you some questions relating to the issue of a forged document. Do you recall that question; yes or no?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-033
utterances.text: Yes, I recall it.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: When did you possess that forged document or ID? Do you recall the year that you possessed it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-033
utterances.text: I think it was in the year 2000. It was around the year 2000. I had a pistol and an ID which I found and I put my picture on it, because I was going to Montenegro and I wanted to have it in case I was checked. I wanted to have some sort of document on me, because at that time I was supposed to be serving a prison sentence, but I was at large.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Have you been to court and received a judgement with respect to that forged identification?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-033
utterances.text: The Statue of Limitations applied, it's seven years, because I hid from the police for seven, seven and a half years. And as I went before the Investigating Judge, I was issued with a decision stating that the Statue of Limitations applied to that offence. And later on, I was sentenced to four years, but I was on provisional release, because the prosecutor indicted me for a false ID. And I went to court and I was sentenced to four years in prison, but this was -- I was on provisional release. It was a suspended sentence.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Objection, before we move into private session. Judges, I feel that you have to intervene. How was this witness available to the OTP in 2004, in 2006, when he was not available to the Serbian police? From 2000 to 2007, he was inaccessible to the Serbian police, but he was accessible to the OTP of The Hague Tribunal. I feel that you have to clarify this ex officio.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, this is exactly what spoke to my mind when I heard you. You were sentenced to four years in jail, obviously, and you were -- you escaped this. A fugitive. Now, there's a Statue of Limitations which has applied. I believe that in your country the Statue of Limitations is three years or something, but I have to check that. So when you arrived at the Tribunal with the investigators in 2004, were you still wanted?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I hadn't been sentenced to four years in prison at that time. I knew that the police would be looking for me because of the pistol and the false ID, so I hid in order for the Statue of Limitations to apply, because I hadn't been in contact with the Investigating Judge. I contacted the ITP [as interpreted] through Ljubisa Petkovic. He arranged my contact with the investigators of The Hague Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But when you were in contact with The Hague investigators, were you still wanted by the police of your country, and did the investigator know about this?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I told them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Did he give you guarantees?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, they didn't. I just made the statement and went on my way.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: When did you receive the four years probation for having the forged ID?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-033
utterances.text: A month ago. I'm not sure of the exact day, I don't have the document with me, but it was a month ago. That's when I was sentenced to four years, and it was a suspended sentence.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Objection. Judges, this was not dealt with either during the examination in chief or the cross-examination, but the OTP should provide an answer to the following: If this witness was previously convicted, how can his sentence be a suspended one when this is not his first offence? Suspended sentences are handed down to people who have committed an offence for the first time, not for repeat offenders. So let this be clarified.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Madam Biersay.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: I'm not in a position to clarify that. I'm not an expert on Serbian law. We disclosed these varied convictions and arrests to Mr. Seselj I believe on Monday, so he was well aware, and he, in his cross-examination, ended with addressing the issue of the forged ID, and that's why I'm clarifying it in redirect.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Please resume.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: If we could please move to private session at this time, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Private session, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we are back in open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. We are in open session. Tomorrow, Mr. Mundis and Ms. Biersay, we will be devoting the session to videos, so you have handed over all of the scripts for the videos, and we shall proceed as last time. We'll look at the video. Mr. Seselj will make his comments, if there are any, and then we go on to the next video, and so on and so forth. Is that what we're going to do tomorrow, Mr. Mundis?

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: It is indeed, Mr. President. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could you just tell me when we're sitting tomorrow, in the morning or the afternoon?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, tomorrow the hearing will be in the afternoon. I can't remember whether it's a quarter past 2.00 or quarter to 3.00. No, it is 2.15 until 6.30. Yes, I can see the assistant nodding. So 2.15 tomorrow afternoon. We could have had the hearing in the morning, but unfortunately my fellow Judges will be in another case and that's why we will be sitting in the afternoon. So apart from the witness, we shall all be meeting again here in the afternoon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
